data.long_meaning: Derived from 'Amar' (immortal) and 'Nath' (god or lord), Amaranaath refers to a god or lord who is considered immortal in Hindu mythology. The name Amaranaath carries the meaning “Immortal God” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Amaranaath usually hope their child will grow to embody immortal god and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.cultural_impact: The name Amaranaath holds significant cultural importance in Hinduism, reflecting the deeply rooted belief in the immortal nature of God or the divine. This concept underscores the eternal and unchanging attribute of God, largely found in various Hindu deities, most notably in Shiva, who is revered as the eternal god. The name invokes a sense of reverence and devotion towards God, underscoring the transcendental and timeless nature of the divine essence in Hindu mythology and philosophy.
data.spiritual_significance: Amaranaath transcends the transitory nature of human existence and embodies the eternal and infinite being. The spiritual significance of the name embodies the profound concept of the absolute reality and the universally present divine consciousness that pervades all existence. The name encourages devotees to seek refuge in the immortal and eternal Lord beyond the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth, ultimately inspiring a quest for spiritual enlightenment and liberation from the conditioned self.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Amaranath signifies the embodiment of eternal love and devotion to Lord Shiva, symbolizing the soul's unending connection to the divine. The name Amaranaath is derived from 'Amar' (immortal) and 'Nath' (lord), representing the belief in the immortal bond between the devotee and the divine master.

historical_references.reference: Amaranath was a renowned Jain Tirthankara of the 12th cycle of Jainism, also known as the Siddhantakaal or the age of the perfected beings. He is believed to have lived between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE in the Indian subcontinent.

Amaranath is also mentioned in the 12th-century Sanskrit epic 'Prabandha Chintamani' by Jaidev. The epic describes Amaranath as a great Jain monk who attained 'Kevala Jnana' (omniscience) and was a disciple of Mahavira, the last Tirthankara of Jainism. The epic also mentions that Amaranath's teachings had a profound influence on Jainism in medieval India.
